title: Inertia and mass
question: What is inertia?

principle.name: Inertia and mass
principle.formulaNote: mass = force ÷ acceleration: the same push changes a heavier thing's motion less. For spinning things, the moment of inertia I = Σ m r² plays the same role.
principle.idea: Everything keeps doing what it is doing, staying still or moving steadily in a straight line, until a force changes it. That stubbornness is inertia, and mass, in kilograms, is how much of it something has.
principle.discovered: 1638–1687 · Galileo's inertia, named by Kepler, made law by Newton

examples.title: Lurching on a braking bus
examples.text: When the bus brakes, nothing has touched you yet, so you carry on at the old speed. Standing without holding on, most people tip at about 1.3 m/s² of braking.

examples.title: Seat belts and airbags
examples.text: In a crash the car stops in about a tenth of a second and you don't, unless the belt and airbag slow you with it, over as long a distance as possible.

examples.title: The engine's flywheel
examples.text: A four-cylinder engine pushes in two bursts every turn. The flywheel's rotational inertia stores each burst and hands it back, so the crankshaft turns smoothly.

examples.title: Braking on a motorcycle
examples.text: With no seat belt, a rider's arms, knees and seat must hold back their whole body: about 500 N for a 70 kg rider braking at 7 m/s².

examples.title: Light wheels feel quick
examples.text: A bicycle wheel's mass sits far out in the rim, so it counts four times over in its moment of inertia. Lighter rims make a bike easier to spin up and slow down.

examples.title: The washing machine drum
examples.text: A heavy drum takes time to spin up to 1,200 rpm and to stop. An unbalanced lump of wet clothes makes it shake, which is why the machine redistributes the load first.

examples.title: Tying down lorry loads
examples.text: Friction can only hold a crate while braking stays under μ g, about 3 m/s² on bare steel, whatever it weighs. Rules require straps rated for 0.8 g forwards.

examples.title: The tablecloth trick
examples.text: Yank the cloth fast and friction drags each plate for only a tenth of a second or so. Its inertia means it moves just a couple of centimetres.

examples.title: Weighing astronauts
examples.text: Scales don't work in orbit, so ISS astronauts sit on SLAMMD: springs pull them with a known force, a sensor measures the acceleration, and m = F ÷ a.

hook: Why do you lurch when the bus brakes, and how does a coin drop neatly into a glass when you flick the card away? Push carts, yank a tablecloth, spin a skater, hang a bicycle wheel from a string, weigh an astronaut without weight, and test the most precise coincidence in physics.

explainer.title: Hard to budge
explainer.text: Inertia is how hard it is to change something's motion, and mass, in kilograms, measures it: the same force gives half the acceleration to twice the mass, a = F ÷ m. Mass is not weight: weight is m g, in newtons, and changes on the Moon. Flick a card or yank a tablecloth fast and inertia keeps the coin and plates where they were.

explainer.title: Riding
explainer.text: When a bus brakes, you keep going until something pushes you back with F = m a: about 180 N for a 60 kg passenger at 3 m/s². Unaided, you tip beyond about 1.3 m/s². Seat belts, a rider's arms and lorry straps all supply that force; friction alone can hold a load only up to μ g.

explainer.title: Spinning
explainer.text: For turning, inertia is the moment of inertia I = Σ m r². A skater pulling her arms in cuts I nearly four times, so she spins nearly four times faster, keeping L = I ω. A spinning wheel hung from a string precesses instead of falling, and a flywheel smooths an engine's power strokes.

explainer.title: Measuring mass
explainer.text: A spring scale measures weight and reads a sixth on the Moon; a balance compares masses and reads true, but fails in orbit. Skylab's crews wobbled on a spring chair (T = 2π √(m ÷ k)); the ISS's SLAMMD pulls with a known force and computes m = F ÷ a.

explainer.title: Myths and limits
explainer.text: Things don't naturally slow down: friction stops them, and on ice a heavy sledge slides as far as a light one. Inertial and gravitational mass agree to 1 part in 10¹⁵ (MICROSCOPE, 2022), the equivalence principle behind general relativity. 'Relativistic mass' is an old idea; mass today means rest mass.

concepts.def: The tendency of an object to keep still, or keep moving in a straight line at steady speed, until a force acts.
The amount of inertia an object has, measured in kilograms: m = F ÷ a.
The pull of gravity on a mass, W = m g, in newtons. It changes from place to place; mass does not.
The SI unit of mass, defined since 2019 by fixing the Planck constant at 6.626 070 15 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s.
Resistance to changes in spin, I = Σ m r², in kg·m². Mass far from the axis counts most.
L = I ω. It stays constant unless a torque acts, which is why skaters spin faster with arms in.
A mass on springs whose wobble period, T = 2π √(m ÷ k), measures mass without gravity.
Inertial and gravitational mass are the same, so everything falls alike. Tested to about 1 part in 10¹⁵.
